label: confounding by indication
text: PITFALL: Confounding by indication - statins are preferentially prescribed to patients with cardiovascular risk, diabetes or CKD, who have higher baseline creatinine, so in a cross-sectional cohort statin users can look worse (or better, if CKD patients are taken off statins) regardless of any drug effect. CHECK: compare AGE, SEX, BMI, ECOG_PS by STATIN_USE and see whether the crude and adjusted creatinine differences agree in direction. IF FOUND: base the verdict on the covariate-adjusted (and SITE-adjusted) estimate, and say the design is observational and cannot show causation; the hypothesis only asks whether users have lower creatinine, so an adjusted association is enough to decide the label. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwg231 (Ray, new-user designs / confounding by indication) (not re-verified; search tool returned HTTP 403).

label: missing and sentinel values
text: PITFALL: Missing or blank SERUM_CREATININE / STATIN_USE values (NA, empty strings, codes like -1 or 999) handled silently by pandas, or missing more often at one site or in one statin group, can bias the comparison. CHECK: count missing and sentinel values of SERUM_CREATININE and STATIN_USE overall, by STATIN_USE and by SITE; check that PATIENT_ID is unique in the patient table. IF FOUND: use a complete-case analysis and report n per group; if missingness differs by group or site, add a sensitivity analysis and adjust for SITE. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.b2393 (Sterne et al., missing data guidance) (not re-verified; search tool returned HTTP 403).

label: ER coding inverted
text: PITFALL: ER_STATUS in data_clinical_supplement.txt is coded 1 = negative, 0 = positive (inverted from the usual convention), so reading 1 as positive flips the direction of the result. CHECK: cross-tabulate ER_STATUS against ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE; ER-negative (1) rows should have percent 0 (or <1%). IF FOUND inconsistent rows: define ER group from the documented coding and confirm with percent; report direction as ER-negative minus ER-positive. SOURCE: column header of data_clinical_supplement.txt; ASCO/CAP ER testing guideline (Allison et al., J Clin Oncol 2020, 1% cutoff), https://doi.org/10.1200/JCO.19.02309

label: Site confounding of calcium
text: PITFALL: Serum calcium was measured at different hospital sites (SITE column says the site ran the blood tests); if site has a calibration offset and ER mix differs by site, a crude ER comparison is confounded (Simpson's paradox). CHECK: tabulate ER status by SITE and compare mean SERUM_CALCIUM by SITE; then compare ER groups within each site. IF FOUND site differences: use a regression of calcium on ER status adjusted for SITE (fixed effect) or a stratified test, and base the label on the adjusted estimate, reporting crude vs adjusted. SOURCE: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox (unverified, search unavailable)

label: ER coding inverted
text: PITFALL: In data_clinical_patient.txt the ER_STATUS column is coded 1 = negative, 0 = positive (per the column description line), so reading 1 as positive flips the direction of any ER comparison. CHECK: Read the '#' description rows; cross-tabulate ER_STATUS against ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE (negatives should have 0%). IF FOUND: Recode explicitly to ER_POS = (ER_STATUS==0) before any analysis, and flag rows where status and percent disagree. SOURCE: data dictionary in the file header (web search unavailable).

label: Albumin correction of calcium
text: PITFALL: Total serum calcium depends on serum albumin (about 0.8 mg/dL per 1 g/dL albumin); if albumin differs between ER groups, a total-calcium difference may reflect albumin, not calcium status. CHECK: compare SERUM_ALBUMIN between ER groups and correlation of calcium with albumin. IF FOUND: also analyse albumin-corrected calcium = Ca + 0.8*(4.0 - albumin) or adjust for albumin in regression; report whether the conclusion holds for both total and corrected calcium. SOURCE: Payne et al., BMJ 1973, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.4.5893.643 (unverified, search unavailable)

label: Site confounding of blood tests
text: PITFALL: The SITE column is the hospital that enrolled the patient AND ran the blood tests, so site-level assay calibration or case-mix differences can create or hide an ER-vs-glucose difference (confounding / Simpson's paradox if ER mix differs by site). CHECK: Tabulate ER-positive fraction by site and glucose mean/median by site; compare the pooled ER difference with the within-site differences. IF FOUND: Base the conclusion on a site-stratified or site-adjusted model (e.g. glucose ~ ER + site, or site fixed effects / per-site z-scores), not the pooled comparison. SOURCE: standard confounding/Simpson's paradox guidance, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox (not retrieved; search tool failed).

label: Units and outliers in calcium
text: PITFALL: Clinical values may contain implausible entries, unit mix-ups (calcium in mmol/L ~2.2-2.6 vs mg/dL ~8.5-10.5; albumin g/L vs g/dL) or sentinel codes (e.g. -1, 999), which can drive a mean difference. CHECK: summarise SERUM_CALCIUM and SERUM_ALBUMIN range per SITE; look for values far outside 7-14 mg/dL or a cluster near 2-3. IF FOUND: convert units (mg/dL = mmol/L * 4.008) or set sentinels to missing, and use a robust test (Mann-Whitney) alongside the t-test. SOURCE: standard clinical lab reference ranges (unverified, search unavailable)

label: Glucose unit mixing
text: PITFALL: Fasting glucose is labelled mg/dL but some sites may have recorded mmol/L (values ~3-15 instead of ~60-250; factor 18.016), which badly distorts means. CHECK: Plot/describe FASTING_GLUCOSE by site; look for a cluster of values below ~30. IF FOUND: Convert mmol/L values to mg/dL (multiply by 18.016) or use within-site standardisation, and report the result both ways. SOURCE: clinical chemistry convention 1 mmol/L glucose = 18.016 mg/dL (search tool failed).

label: Missing data by site
text: PITFALL: Missing ER status or calcium may be non-random (e.g. concentrated at one site), and dropping cases silently can bias results. CHECK: count missing ER_STATUS and SERUM_CALCIUM overall and by SITE. IF FOUND: report complete-case n per group and check the result is consistent within sites with complete data. SOURCE: Sterne et al., BMJ 2009 multiple imputation guidance, https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.b2393 (unverified)

label: Age/BMI confounding of glucose
text: PITFALL: Fasting glucose rises with age and BMI, and ER-positive breast cancer patients tend to be older (often postmenopausal), so a crude ER-positive excess in glucose may be explained by age/BMI rather than ER. CHECK: Compare AGE and BMI (supplement file, join on PATIENT_ID) between ER groups; fit glucose ~ ER + age + BMI (+ site). IF FOUND: Report the adjusted ER coefficient alongside the crude one; if the crude difference disappears after adjustment, the hypothesis as a causal/independent claim is not supported, but state clearly what the crude comparison shows. SOURCE: standard epidemiological confounding adjustment (search tool failed).

label: Reverse-coded statin variable
text: PITFALL: STATIN_USE in data_clinical_patient.txt is reverse-coded per its own column description (1 = NOT taking statins, 0 = taking statins); reading 1 as 'user' flips the sign of the effect and the label. CHECK: read the '#' description line, and cross-tabulate STATIN_USE against STATIN_DOSE_MG (users should have dose > 0); report any inconsistent rows. IF FOUND: define statin user from the documented coding (confirmed by dose), state the direction explicitly in reasoning, and exclude or flag rows where code and dose disagree. SOURCE: data dictionary line in /planted-data/data_clinical_patient.txt (no web source; research tool unavailable).

label: Duplicate patients / sample-level join
text: PITFALL: Joining the sample table (multiple samples per patient, primary and metastasis) to patient-level glucose duplicates patients and inflates n and significance. CHECK: Verify PATIENT_ID is unique in the patient file and count samples per patient; check for duplicated patient rows. IF FOUND: Analyse glucose at the patient level only (one row per patient); deduplicate and do not use sample-level rows for a patient-level outcome. SOURCE: general data-handling practice (search tool failed).

label: Direction and decision rule
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis is directional (ER-negative LOWER calcium); a significant difference in the opposite direction should be labelled False, and a null result is not automatically True. CHECK: report the adjusted mean difference (ER-neg minus ER-pos) with 95% CI and p-value. IF FOUND: label True only if the adjusted difference is negative and significant; False if clearly no difference or the opposite direction with adequate power. SOURCE: general hypothesis-testing practice (no link)

label: Site confounding of lab values
text: PITFALL: SITE is the hospital that both enrolled patients and ran the blood tests, so site-level lab calibration differences and site-level differences in TP53 mutation mix can create or reverse a pooled cholesterol difference (confounding / Simpson's paradox). CHECK: cross-tab TP53_STATUS by SITE and compare mean TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL by SITE; compute the TP53 difference within each site. IF FOUND site imbalance or site cholesterol offsets: base the conclusion on a site-adjusted model (cholesterol ~ TP53 + SITE, or stratified/within-site comparison), not the pooled t-test. SOURCE: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpson%27s_paradox

label: Samples per patient / pseudoreplication
text: PITFALL: The IFN-gamma score is per sample, the exposure per patient; patients may contribute several samples (primary and metastasis), so a sample-level t-test is pseudoreplication and overstates significance. CHECK: count samples per PATIENT_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt and check for orphan IDs that do not join to the patient table. IF FOUND: analyse one value per patient (e.g. primary sample only, or patient mean) or use a mixed model with a patient random effect; report sample-level results only as a sensitivity check. SOURCE: Lazic 2010, BMC Neuroscience 11:5, https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2202-11-5 (not retrieved; research tool unavailable).

label: Directional hypothesis and evidence label
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis is directional (ER-positive higher); a non-significant difference is not evidence against it, while a significant difference in the opposite direction is. CHECK: Report effect size with 95% CI, the sign of (ER+ minus ER-) after correct recoding, and whether conclusions agree between crude and site/age/BMI-adjusted analyses. IF FOUND: Label True only if the ER+ excess is robust; False if the data show no difference with a tight CI or the opposite direction robustly; avoid Not verifiable because the relevant variables exist. SOURCE: standard inference practice (search tool failed).

label: Processing batch confounding
text: PITFALL: Expression-assay scores can be dominated by PROCESSING_BATCH; if statin users are unevenly spread across batches, a crude difference can be a batch artefact or, after adjustment, reverse (Simpson's paradox). CHECK: cross-tab statin status by PROCESSING_BATCH and compare IFNG score by batch; fit IFNG ~ statin + batch. IF FOUND: base the conclusion on the batch-adjusted or within-batch-stratified estimate, not the crude one. SOURCE: Leek et al. 2010, Nat Rev Genet 11:733, https://doi.org/10.1038/nrg2825 (not retrieved; research tool unavailable).

label: Purity-driven TP53 misclassification
text: PITFALL: Low tumour purity makes truly mutant tumours look TP53 wild type (false-negative calls when VAF falls below detection), diluting or distorting the comparison. CHECK: compare TUMOR_PURITY between TP53 groups (sample table, join on PATIENT_ID) and rerun the comparison restricted to purity >= ~0.2-0.3 or adjusted for purity. IF FOUND the effect changes in high-purity samples: give weight to the purity-restricted/adjusted estimate. SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1038/nbt.2514

label: ER percent inconsistency and sex
text: PITFALL: ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE may conflict with ER_STATUS (e.g. status positive with 0%, or under the 1% ASCO/CAP threshold), and the cohort may include male patients. CHECK: Cross-tab status vs percent (ASCO/CAP: >=1% staining = positive) and tabulate SEX. IF FOUND: Run a sensitivity analysis defining ER from the percentage (>=1%) and with/without male patients; report if the label changes. SOURCE: ASCO/CAP ER testing guideline, Allison et al. J Clin Oncol 2020 (not retrieved; search tool failed).

label: Tumour purity confounding
text: PITFALL: Bulk immune signatures such as IFN-gamma scores fall as tumour purity rises (less immune infiltrate), so a group difference in TUMOR_PURITY can make or hide an IFNG difference. CHECK: correlate TUMOR_PURITY with IFNG_SIGNATURE_SCORE and compare purity between statin groups. IF FOUND: adjust for purity in a regression (IFNG ~ statin + purity + batch + sample type) and report whether the statin estimate changes in sign or size. SOURCE: Aran, Sirota & Butte 2015, Nat Commun 6:8971, https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms9971 (not retrieved; research tool unavailable).

label: Demographic/BMI confounding
text: PITFALL: Cholesterol is confounded by age, sex and BMI (supplement table), which may also differ by TP53 group. CHECK: compare AGE, SEX, BMI across TP53 groups; fit cholesterol ~ TP53 + SITE + AGE + SEX + BMI. IF FOUND the adjusted and crude estimates disagree in sign or significance: report the adjusted one, but do not adjust for post-diagnosis variables that could be mediators. SOURCE: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK236/

label: Sample type confounding
text: PITFALL: SAMPLE_TYPE (primary vs metastasis) changes the immune microenvironment, and metastases may be over-represented in one exposure group, which confounds the comparison. CHECK: cross-tab sample type by statin status and compare IFNG by sample type. IF FOUND: stratify by sample type or restrict to primaries, plus a sensitivity analysis. SOURCE: general confounding principle, Hernan & Robins, Causal Inference: What If, https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/miguel-hernan/causal-inference-book/ (not retrieved; research tool unavailable).

label: Site and healthy-user confounding; cholesterol as mediator
text: PITFALL: Hospital SITE ran the blood tests and may have enrolled patients with different statin prescribing, so site can confound patient-level comparisons. Statin users also differ systematically (age, cholesterol, comorbidity; healthy-user and indication bias). CHECK: cross-tab statin by SITE; compare AGE, SEX, TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL, ECOG_PS and BMI by statin group. IF FOUND: include SITE and key covariates in an adjusted model; do not adjust for TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL as a plain confounder because statins lower it (it is a mediator/collider), and report it only as a sensitivity analysis. SOURCE: Shrank, Patrick & Brookhart 2011, J Gen Intern Med 26:546, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-010-1609-1 (not retrieved; research tool unavailable).

label: Duplicates and join errors
text: PITFALL: Duplicate patient rows, multiple samples per patient (e.g. primary plus metastasis), or unmatched IDs across the three tables inflate n or drop patients when joining. CHECK: count unique PATIENT_ID in each file, check SAMPLE_TYPE values and samples per patient, and do left joins with row counts before and after. IF FOUND: analyse at one row per patient (cholesterol and TP53 are patient-level) and deduplicate before testing. SOURCE: https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/#clinical-data

label: Interpreting null vs contradicting evidence
text: PITFALL: Deciding the label from p<0.05 alone mixes up 'no evidence' and 'evidence against'. A non-significant or opposite-direction result means different things. CHECK: report the effect estimate with its 95% CI, both crude and adjusted, plus a nonparametric test (Mann-Whitney), and check outliers and missing IFNG values. IF FOUND: label True only if users are robustly higher; label False if the estimate is clearly null or reversed with relevant variables present. Not verifiable fits only when the variables are missing, and here they are present. SOURCE: Wasserstein & Lazar 2016, ASA statement on p-values, https://doi.org/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108 (not retrieved; research tool unavailable).

label: Unit/sentinel cholesterol values
text: PITFALL: Implausible or sentinel cholesterol values (e.g. 0, -1, 999, values in mmol/L ~3-8 mixed with mg/dL ~120-300, possibly from one site) distort means. CHECK: describe TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL overall and by SITE, look for NA, sentinels and a bimodal mmol/L cluster. IF FOUND: convert mmol/L to mg/dL (x38.67) or exclude with justification, and use a robust test (Mann-Whitney/rank-based regression) as a sensitivity check. SOURCE: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK351/

QUESTION: When a multi-site comparison has one site with very few controls and a within-site estimate opposite in sign to the others, what is the recommended way to pool: fixed effects, random effects, or Mantel-Haenszel-style stratified estimation? What heterogeneity test p-value threshold is conventionally used? ANSWER: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on every call (2 in this session, 3 in an earlier one), so no page could be read. From standard meta-analysis practice (Cochrane Handbook ch.10, recalled, not read): with few sites and one sparse site, use a fixed-effect stratified estimate. That means Mantel-Haenszel for binary outcomes; for a continuous outcome like cholesterol, use inverse-variance weighting or a regression with site as a fixed effect. Random effects is less suitable here: the between-site variance cannot be estimated reliably from few sites, and random effects shifts weight toward the small, noisy site. Test heterogeneity with Cochran's Q (chi-squared) at P < 0.10, rather than 0.05, because the test has low power. Report I^2 alongside it (about 25/50/75% = low/moderate/high). If Q is not significant, the opposite-sign estimate in the sparse site is consistent with chance. As sensitivity checks, report a leave-the-sparse-site-out estimate and a random-effects estimate. So when the variables exist and the data do not show the claimed direction (especially when the estimate points the other way), the usual label is False, not Not verifiable. HOW SURE: low. reason: If the groups are read the wrong way round, the conclusion flips. The teams need to check the coding against the data rather than trust a convention or a single legend.
text: How TP53_STATUS is coded decides which way the result points. Do not assume the usual 1 = mutant convention. Read the '#' description lines for TP53_STATUS and TP53_VAF in data_clinical_patient.txt, then cross-tabulate TP53_STATUS against TP53_VAF (zero vs non-zero) to check whether the data match the stated legend. If the legend and the data disagree, check the metadata against the measurements themselves, report the discrepancy, and say which coding you used and why. Call the grouping unresolved (Not verifiable) only if no internal evidence can tell the codings apart.

reason: This gives an internal way to confirm which group is wild type, and guards against purity-driven misclassification diluting the comparison.
text: Tumour purity gives an independent check on TP53 calls (unverified background knowledge). A wild-type tumour should have VAF 0 or below the detection limit. A clonal heterozygous somatic mutation should have VAF around purity/2, and up to about purity with LOH or copy gain. VAFs far above purity suggest germline variants or errors. Low purity can also make mutant tumours look wild type. Join TUMOR_PURITY from the sample table, check VAF against purity in each group, compare purity between groups, and rerun the comparison restricted to purity >= about 0.2-0.3 (or adjusted for purity).

reason: Site confounding could change which estimate should be primary.
text: SITE is the hospital that both enrolled patients and ran the blood tests. Lab calibration differences and differences in TP53 mix between sites could create or reverse a pooled cholesterol difference (Simpson's paradox). Cross-tabulate TP53 group by SITE, compare TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL by SITE, and estimate the TP53 difference within each site. If sites are imbalanced or offset, base the conclusion on a site-adjusted model (cholesterol ~ TP53 + SITE) or a within-site comparison.

reason: Confounding by demographics or body size could change the direction or significance of the difference.
text: Age, sex and BMI (BMI is in data_clinical_supplement.txt) affect cholesterol and may differ between TP53 groups. Compare them across groups and fit cholesterol ~ TP53 + SITE + AGE + SEX + BMI. If the crude and adjusted estimates disagree in sign or significance, report the adjusted one. Do not adjust for post-diagnosis variables that could be mediators.

reason: Without unit harmonisation, a spurious difference in cholesterol could drive the label.
text: Some rows report labs in SI units and the rest in mg/dL. In SI rows cholesterol is about 4-6 mmol/L, against 130-230 mg/dL elsewhere, and this appears to be tied to SITE C1. Mixing the two creates a huge artefactual group difference. Summarise TOTAL_CHOLESTEROL (and SERUM_CALCIUM, FASTING_GLUCOSE) by SITE and flag cholesterol < 20. reason: This decides which estimate the conclusion should rest on.
text: SITE may confound the comparison: the share of patients who received radiotherapy and the lab units/method may both differ by site, so a pooled difference can reverse or vanish within sites (Simpson's paradox). Cross-tabulate radiotherapy by SITE, compute the cholesterol difference within each site after unit harmonisation, and report a site-stratified or SITE fixed-effect estimate as the primary result.

reason: This tells the team how to pool unbalanced sites and how to read a discordant stratum.
text: If one site has very few patients in one radiotherapy group, and its within-site estimate has the opposite sign, prefer a fixed-effect stratified estimate (regression with SITE as a fixed effect, or inverse-variance weighting for a continuous outcome). Random effects is unreliable with few sites and gives more weight to the small, noisy site. Test heterogeneity with Cochran's Q at P < 0.10 together with I^2, or with an RT*SITE interaction test. If heterogeneity is not significant, a sign flip in a sparse stratum is consistent with chance. Report each within-site estimate with its CI, plus leave-the-sparse-site-out and random-effects sensitivity estimates. This guidance is recalled from standard practice (Cochrane Handbook ch.10); no source was verified.

text: In data_clinical_patient.txt the '#' description line defines ER_STATUS as 1 = negative and 0 = positive. reason: Misclassified exposure or a mixed-sex cohort could change the estimated ER difference.
text: ER_PERCENT_POSITIVE may disagree with ER_STATUS (e.g. 'positive' with 0% or below the ASCO/CAP 1% threshold), and the cohort may include men. Tabulate status against percentage and tabulate SEX; as a sensitivity analysis, define ER from percentage >= 1% and repeat with and without male patients, reporting whether the conclusion changes.

reason: If ER mix differs by site, site lab offsets can create, hide or reverse a pooled ER difference (Simpson's paradox); an additive site term alone may not remove it.
text: SITE is the hospital that both enrolled the patient and ran the blood tests, so assay calibration and case mix can differ by site. Tabulate the ER-positive fraction and the glucose distribution (mean, median, SD) by site and compare the pooled ER difference with within-site differences. Base the conclusion on a site-adjusted or site-stratified estimate (glucose ~ ER + SITE). Because lab-to-lab differences can be proportional or change variance, not only shift the mean, also check robustness with within-site standardisation (per-site z-scores or log glucose with site effects) or a site-by-ER interaction (this last point is from unverified background knowledge, low-medium confidence).

reason: A crude ER difference may be explained by age/BMI; the teams need both estimates to judge the claim.
text: Fasting glucose rises with age and BMI, and ER-positive patients tend to be older. reason: Mixed units would badly distort group means, especially when ER mix differs by site.
text: FASTING_GLUCOSE is labelled mg/dL, but a site may have recorded mmol/L (values around 3-15 instead of 60-250). Describe glucose by site and look for a cluster below about 30; if present, convert (mg/dL = mmol/L x 18.016) or standardise within site, and report results both ways.

reason: Sentinels silently entering means could create or mask a group difference.

reason: Duplicated patients inflate n and false significance.
text: Glucose is a patient-level variable, while the sample table can hold several samples per patient (primary and metastasis). Confirm PATIENT_ID is unique in the patient table and analyse one row per patient; do not join sample rows onto the glucose outcome.

reason: Interpreting a null or opposite-direction result is the main point where the choice of label can go wrong.
text: The hypothesis is directional (ER-positive higher). Report the sign and size of the ER+ minus ER- difference with a 95% CI, and whether crude and adjusted analyses agree. A non-significant difference and a difference in the opposite direction are different kinds of evidence; a one-sided test or a check of whether the CI excludes a meaningful positive effect helps tell them apart. 'Not verifiable' in this task is defined as the data lacking the relevant variables, so decide the label from what the estimates and their CIs actually show.

QUESTION: In hypothesis testing for a directional claim (group A has lower mean than group B), what is the accepted way to conclude that data contradict the claim rather than being merely inconclusive, e.g. equivalence/non-inferiority testing with a pre-specified margin versus a one-sided confidence bound? ANSWER: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the research gateway returned HTTP 403 on all 3 calls, so no page was read. From standard practice (recalled, not read): a non-significant result is inconclusive on its own, because absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. To conclude the data contradict 'A lower than B' you need one of two things: (a) a significant difference in the opposite direction, or (b) evidence that any meaningful lowering is ruled out. For (b), the one-sided 95% confidence bound for (A minus B) must lie above minus delta, where delta is the smallest lowering that matters and is set in advance. This is the same as a TOST or non-inferiority test with margin delta. A one-sided bound only means something when it is compared with a margin. If the interval still includes a meaningful lowering, the result is inconclusive, not contradicting. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: none given.

QUESTION: When pooling stratum-specific effects across a small number of strata (e.g. three) with borderline heterogeneity, what is the recommended choice between fixed-effect and random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird versus Hartung-Knapp) pooling, and how reliable is DerSimonian-Laird with very few strata? ANSWER: NOT WEB-VERIFIED: the gateway returned HTTP 403, so no page was read. From standard practice (recalled, not read): with about 3 strata, tau^2 (the between-stratum variance) is estimated very poorly. DerSimonian-Laird intervals then tend to be too narrow and miss the true value more often than they should, and DL often sets tau^2 to 0, which gives the same answer as fixed-effect pooling. Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman, using t on k-1 degrees of freedom, is recommended over DL (Cochrane Handbook v6 ch.10; IntHout et al. 2014). With k=3, though, it gives very wide and possibly overly conservative intervals. If the strata are fixed, pre-specified sites within one study, a fixed-effect stratified estimate is defensible: it answers 'what is the average effect in these sites?' With borderline heterogeneity it should still be reported next to a random-effects (HK) sensitivity analysis. If the conclusion changes depending on the pooling method, it is not robust and should be reported as uncertain. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: none given.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In observational studies, should a variable measured after exposure assignment (such as follow-up duration) be included as an adjustment covariate when estimating an association between a baseline exposure and a baseline biomarker, and what bias can it introduce? ANSWER: Generally no. Adjustment covariates should be pre-exposure variables that could confound the exposure-outcome relation. Follow-up duration is measured after baseline, so it cannot cause a baseline biomarker and is not a confounder. If exposure or outcome affects it (for example statin users or high-proliferation patients being followed for different lengths of time, or follow-up reflecting survival or censoring), conditioning on it can cause collider/selection bias or overadjustment bias (Schisterman et al. 2009). At best it adds noise. Treat the crude or pre-exposure-adjusted estimate as primary and the follow-up-adjusted estimate only as a sensitivity check; if the two disagree, trust the one without follow-up. ANSWER: Not settled by the web (gateway HTTP 403). Unverified background: for a clonal heterozygous SNV in a diploid region, expected VAF is about purity/2. LOH can raise it up to about purity, and mutant-allele amplification can raise it further, but VAF clearly above purity should be uncommon. For TP53, which often comes with 17p LOH, VAF between purity/2 and purity is common. VAF > purity in about 40% of cases is not expected and suggests purity underestimation, germline variants, or an unreliable VAF or purity column. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: none given.

QUESTION: Are TP53-mutant solid tumours typically associated with shorter survival, higher hypoxia signatures or different interferon-gamma signatures than TP53 wild-type tumours? ANSWER: Not settled by the web (gateway HTTP 403). Unverified background: TP53 mutation is often reported to go with worse survival in many solid tumours, but this depends on cancer type. text: REPLY (purity): re-run on 161 status-1 patients gives Spearman rho(VAF, purity) = -0.12 (p=0.15) and VAF > purity in 39%. This weakens rather than backs trusting VAF as a real somatic measurement, but it does not support the opposite coding either: it bears on how realistic the VAF values are, not on which group carries the variant.

text: REPLY (adjusted model): OLS with site, batch, age, sex, BMI, ECOG, sample type and purity gives status-1 minus status-0 cholesterol +34.7 mg/dL (95% CI 27.0-42.4, p=4e-17). Glucose (p=0.36), creatinine (p=0.21), BMI, age, ECOG and purity do not differ by group. The gap and its sign are unchanged.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY (both codings, and the pre-stated rule): Under VAF coding (status 1 = mutant), wild type has 154.7 vs mutant 189.9 mg/dL, so the label is False. Under the stated legend (status 1 = wild type), wild type has 189.9 vs 154.7, so the label is True. No statistical test separates the two codings. The only internal evidence is structural: VAF is exactly 0 in all 172 status-0 patients and >0 in all 161 status-1 patients, and the VAF column's own definition (0 if wild type) agrees with that. The 'legend is right' reading would need a VAF field that is nonzero only in wild-type tumours, which no definition of VAF allows. So two of the three pieces of metadata (VAF values plus VAF legend) agree against the status legend. Separately, the task defines Not verifiable as the data holding no relevant variables, and here the variables exist. I keep False, with confidence about 0.6.

It does not behave like a measured allele fraction, so VAF carries little weight as biology. It still works as a group marker: a 'VAF of the TP53 mutation' that is non-zero only in status 1 and zero in every status-0 row says status 1 = mutant.

label: REPLY
text: REPLY Q(rule for contradicting fields): rule set before looking at cholesterol again: prefer the reading under which the fewest documented statements are wrong, and keep the label that reading gives. Under the status legend (1=WT), the VAF description AND every VAF value would be incoherent, because wild-type tumours would carry mutation VAFs and every mutant would have VAF 0. Under the VAF reading only one sentence, the status legend, is wrong. Applying the rule gives 1 = mutant, and so the same label, False. Not verifiable is kept for data that lack the variables, and here they are present.
